quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: I finished the quarterly report, ___ my manager forwarded it to the client within the hour.
quests.completedSentence: I finished the quarterly report, and my manager forwarded it to the client within the hour.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both clauses stand as equal, matching facts in a sequence, so 'and' links the two full sentences without adding contrast or a result.
quests.nativeTip: Two complete events are simply happening one after the other, with nothing pushing back against either.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: The rain stopped ___ the sun came out almost immediately after.
quests.completedSentence: The rain stopped and the sun came out almost immediately after.
quests.ruleExplanation: The sentence reports two connected facts happening in order, and 'and' is enough to link them without implying cause or contrast.
quests.nativeTip: One weather change simply followed the other, with no clash between the two.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: The landlord fixed the leaking tap ___ replaced the broken window latch the same afternoon.
quests.completedSentence: The landlord fixed the leaking tap and replaced the broken window latch the same afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both repairs were completed by the same person on the same visit, so 'and' simply adds the second task to the first.
quests.nativeTip: The landlord did two separate repair jobs, both getting done.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The interview went smoothly, ___ she still felt nervous the whole time.
quests.completedSentence: The interview went smoothly, but she still felt nervous the whole time.
quests.ruleExplanation: You'd expect the smooth interview to calm her nerves, but it didn't, and 'but' marks that clash between the two clauses.
quests.nativeTip: A smooth interview would normally ease nerves — did that happen here?

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The bakery down the street closed for good, ___ a new one opened just two blocks away within a month.
quests.completedSentence: The bakery down the street closed for good, but a new one opened just two blocks away within a month.
quests.ruleExplanation: A closing bakery seems like a loss, but a new one quickly replacing it undercuts that impression, which 'but' signals.
quests.nativeTip: One shop closing sounds like bad news, so what happened right after undercuts that feeling.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The instructions were written in tiny print, ___ most customers never bothered to read them.
quests.completedSentence: The instructions were written in tiny print, but most customers never bothered to read them.
quests.ruleExplanation: The sentence sets up a contrast between the print's condition and people's behavior toward it, not a cause pushing them to skip it, so 'but' fits better than a result word.
quests.nativeTip: Small print alone doesn't explain why people skipped it — think about what clashes here instead.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Choice
quests.contextSentence: Turn down the music, ___ the neighbors will complain again.
quests.completedSentence: Turn down the music, or the neighbors will complain again.
quests.ruleExplanation: Not turning the music down leads directly to the unwanted outcome, and 'or' is how English sets up that if-you-don't warning.
quests.nativeTip: One path avoids a problem; not taking it leads straight to that problem.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Choice
quests.contextSentence: We can split the bill evenly, ___ each person can pay for exactly what they ordered.
quests.completedSentence: We can split the bill evenly, or each person can pay for exactly what they ordered.
quests.ruleExplanation: Two payment methods are being offered as alternatives, and only one will be chosen, which is exactly the role 'or' plays.
quests.nativeTip: Two different ways to settle the bill are being offered — only one will actually happen.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Choice
quests.contextSentence: Renew your subscription before Friday, ___ your account will be paused automatically.
quests.completedSentence: Renew your subscription before Friday, or your account will be paused automatically.
quests.ruleExplanation: Failing to renew is what causes the pause, and 'or' is the word that connects an action to what happens if it's skipped.
quests.nativeTip: Skipping the first action triggers the second one automatically.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: Two team members called in sick this morning, ___ the project deadline has been pushed to Friday.
quests.completedSentence: Two team members called in sick this morning, so the project deadline has been pushed to Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: The staff shortage led directly to the schedule change, and 'so' introduces that outcome.
quests.nativeTip: The missing staff is the cause; the new deadline is what came out of it.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: The printer jammed twice during the presentation, ___ we switched to sharing the slides on screen instead.
quests.completedSentence: The printer jammed twice during the presentation, so we switched to sharing the slides on screen instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: The repeated jamming is the reason the team switched methods, and 'so' shows that one thing led to the other.
quests.nativeTip: The printer trouble is what forced the change in plan.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: Parking fees doubled near the stadium, ___ many commuters decided to take the bus instead.
quests.completedSentence: Parking fees doubled near the stadium, so many commuters decided to take the bus instead.
quests.ruleExplanation: The parking fee hike directly caused commuters to change their routine, and 'so' introduces that outcome.
quests.nativeTip: The fee hike is the cause; the switch to the bus is what actually happened as a result.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The trail was steep and exhausting, ___ the view from the top made every step worth it.
quests.completedSentence: The trail was steep and exhausting, yet the view from the top made every step worth it.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' introduces a contrast much like 'but', showing that the reward at the top stood despite the hard climb described just before it.
quests.nativeTip: A difficult climb doesn't usually feel worth it — but something changed that here.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: He had rehearsed the speech dozens of times, ___ his voice still shook when he stepped on stage.
quests.completedSentence: He had rehearsed the speech dozens of times, yet his voice still shook when he stepped on stage.
quests.ruleExplanation: The heavy rehearsal makes the shaking voice unexpected, and 'yet' signals that lingering contrast between preparation and outcome.
quests.nativeTip: All that practice should have removed the nerves — did it?

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The company cut its marketing budget in half, ___ sales climbed higher than ever that quarter.
quests.completedSentence: The company cut its marketing budget in half, yet sales climbed higher than ever that quarter.
quests.ruleExplanation: A shrinking budget alongside rising sales is a surprising pairing, and 'yet' is the word that flags that kind of unexpected result.
quests.nativeTip: Less marketing spending would normally mean weaker sales — not stronger ones.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: I didn't get a reply to my email, ___ did anyone answer my phone calls.
quests.completedSentence: I didn't get a reply to my email, nor did anyone answer my phone calls.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both the email and the calls went unanswered, and 'nor' adds a second negative fact to a first one, which is why the verb flips before the subject.
quests.nativeTip: Both attempts at contact failed, and the second one is being added to the first with a matching negative meaning.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: The manager never raised his voice, ___ did he ever lose his patience with a difficult customer.
quests.completedSentence: The manager never raised his voice, nor did he ever lose his patience with a difficult customer.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both parts describe something the manager never did, and 'nor' joins two negative statements, again with the inverted word order that follows it.
quests.nativeTip: Two calm qualities are being listed together, and both are stated as things that didn't happen.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: She doesn't eat meat, ___ does she eat any dairy products.
quests.completedSentence: She doesn't eat meat, nor does she eat any dairy products.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both restrictions are being listed as things she avoids, and 'nor' links two negative clauses while triggering that inverted verb order.
quests.nativeTip: A second food she avoids is being added to the first, both stated in the negative.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Reason
quests.contextSentence: She left the office before the party started, ___ she had promised to pick up her father at the station.
quests.completedSentence: She left the office before the party started, for she had promised to pick up her father at the station.
quests.ruleExplanation: The clause after the comma explains why she left, and 'for' is a more formal, literary way of introducing that reason than 'because'.
quests.nativeTip: The second half of the sentence is explaining the reason behind the first half, in a fairly formal tone.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Reason
quests.contextSentence: The historic clock tower was closed to the public, ___ inspectors had found structural damage in the bell chamber.
quests.completedSentence: The historic clock tower was closed to the public, for inspectors had found structural damage in the bell chamber.
quests.ruleExplanation: The structural damage is the justification for closing the tower, and 'for' introduces that reason in the slightly formal register typical of written reports.
quests.nativeTip: The second clause supplies the justification behind the closing, stated in a formal, report-like tone.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Reason
quests.contextSentence: The committee approved the proposal without much debate, ___ every member had already read the full report beforehand.
quests.completedSentence: The committee approved the proposal without much debate, for every member had already read the full report beforehand.
quests.ruleExplanation: The prior reading is offered as the explanation for the quick approval, and 'for' gives that reason a formal, slightly old-fashioned tone suited to committee language.
quests.nativeTip: The clause after the comma is explaining, in a formal way, why the debate was so short.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: The waiter brought the wrong dish twice, ___ the manager comped our entire meal.
quests.completedSentence: The waiter brought the wrong dish twice, so the manager comped our entire meal.
quests.ruleExplanation: The kitchen's repeated error is the reason behind the free meal, and 'so' shows that outcome following from the mistake.
quests.nativeTip: The repeated mistake is what led the manager to make that decision.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The delivery driver rang the doorbell twice ___ no one answered.
quests.completedSentence: The delivery driver rang the doorbell twice but no one answered.
quests.ruleExplanation: The ringing should have brought someone to the door, but it didn't, and 'but' marks that gap between effort and result.
quests.nativeTip: Ringing twice usually gets someone's attention — did it here?

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Subordinating Conjunctions — Reason
quests.contextSentence: The museum closes early on Sundays ___ the staff need extra time for cleaning before Monday's exhibit.
quests.completedSentence: The museum closes early on Sundays because the staff need extra time for cleaning before Monday's exhibit.
quests.ruleExplanation: The staff's need for extra cleaning time is the reason behind the earlier closing, which is what 'because' introduces here, distinct from the coordinating conjunctions around it.
quests.nativeTip: The cleaning need is the underlying reason for the early closing time.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: The city council rejected the parking proposal, ___ residents flooded the next meeting with complaints.
quests.completedSentence: The city council rejected the parking proposal, so residents flooded the next meeting with complaints.
quests.ruleExplanation: The rejected proposal is the cause of the residents' angry response, and 'so' introduces that direct result.
quests.nativeTip: The rejection is what pushed residents to react the way they did.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: The librarian doesn't allow food near the computers, ___ does she allow drinks without a lid.
quests.completedSentence: The librarian doesn't allow food near the computers, nor does she allow drinks without a lid.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both rules describe things she forbids, and 'nor' adds the second negative rule to the first with the matching inverted structure.
quests.nativeTip: A second banned item is being added to the first, both phrased as things not allowed.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Subordinating Conjunctions — Time
quests.contextSentence: Wait here by the entrance ___ I come back with the car.
quests.completedSentence: Wait here by the entrance until I come back with the car.
quests.ruleExplanation: The waiting is meant to last only up to the moment the car arrives, which is the endpoint meaning carried by 'until', not a coordinating conjunction like the ones around it.
quests.nativeTip: The waiting should continue right up to one clear stopping point.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Result
quests.contextSentence: The flight was overbooked, ___ the airline offered vouchers to anyone willing to take a later one.
quests.completedSentence: The flight was overbooked, so the airline offered vouchers to anyone willing to take a later one.
quests.ruleExplanation: The overbooking directly caused the airline's response, and 'so' introduces that resulting action.
quests.nativeTip: The overbooking is the problem behind the airline's offer.

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Contrast
quests.contextSentence: The intern hadn't touched a spreadsheet before this job, ___ she picked up the formulas within a week.
quests.completedSentence: The intern hadn't touched a spreadsheet before this job, yet she picked up the formulas within a week.
quests.ruleExplanation: Learning that fast despite having no background is the surprising part, and 'yet' is what flags that gap between expectation and reality.
quests.nativeTip: No experience usually means a slow start — did that happen here?

quests.conceptTitle: Traffic Lights of Logic: Coordinating Conjunctions — Addition
quests.contextSentence: He never checks his messages after six, ___ does he answer work calls once he's left the office.
quests.completedSentence: He never checks his messages after six, nor does he answer work calls once he's left the office.
quests.ruleExplanation: Both statements describe something he avoids after work, and 'nor' links these two negative habits with its familiar inverted word order.
quests.nativeTip: A second evening habit is being added to the first, both framed as things he doesn't do.
